name: Apollo 12

terrain.note: Generic moon surface — no site-specific DTM available yet

keyDiscovery: Demonstrated precision landing capability by touching down just 163 metres from the unmanned Surveyor 3 probe, proving astronauts could target specific lunar features.
missionLegacy: Proved that pinpoint lunar landings were achievable, a capability critical for targeting the scientifically interesting terrain of later Apollo missions.
funFact: The Saturn V was struck by lightning twice during launch — at 36 and 52 seconds — briefly knocking out telemetry, but flight controller John Aaron saved the mission with the legendary call 'SCE to AUX.'
heritageNote: The site preserves both Apollo 12 hardware and the Surveyor 3 probe (landed April 1967); the retrieved Surveyor camera is displayed at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. NASA's 2011 heritage guidelines recommend preserving this dual-era site.

objects.name: Intrepid Descent Stage
objects.description: Lower half of Lunar Module Intrepid. Conrad and Bean landed just 163 metres from their target — the unmanned Surveyor 3 probe that had been sitting on the Moon since April 1967.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Validated the precision landing guidance system that allowed subsequent missions to target scientifically valuable terrain features.
objects.legacy: Remains in the Ocean of Storms; its ascent stage was deliberately crashed into the Moon to calibrate the Apollo 12 seismometer.
objects.firstPerson: I am the descent stage of Intrepid. Pete Conrad flew me to a pinpoint landing just 163 metres from Surveyor 3 — exactly where we planned. When my upper half launched away, NASA deliberately crashed it into the Moon so the seismometer could feel the impact. I still stand here, proof that humans could land on a dime.

objects.name: American Flag
objects.description: Planted by Conrad and Bean during EVA-1. Like all Apollo flags, it has a horizontal rod to keep it extended. Bleached white by decades of UV radiation.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Served as a visual reference point in photographs, helping scientists reconstruct the precise layout and distances of the EVA work area.
objects.legacy: LROC images suggest the flag may have been knocked over by the ascent engine exhaust during departure from the surface.
objects.firstPerson: I am the second American flag on the Moon. Pete and Al planted me near Intrepid during their first moonwalk. Like my sister flag at Tranquility Base, I have been baking in unfiltered sunlight for over fifty years. I may have fallen when Intrepid's ascent engine blasted off — no one has visited to check.

objects.name: ALSEP Central Station
objects.description: The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package — a suite of scientific instruments powered by a plutonium-238 RTG. Included a seismometer, magnetometer, solar wind spectrometer, and more. Transmitted data to Earth until September 1977.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Its seismometer detected the deliberate crash of the Intrepid ascent stage, producing vibrations that rang for nearly an hour — revealing the Moon's highly fractured upper crust.
objects.legacy: Transmitted data continuously for nearly eight years until NASA shut down all ALSEP stations on 30 September 1977 to save budget.
objects.firstPerson: I am the ALSEP — a whole science station powered by the heat of plutonium-238. My seismometer felt the crash of Intrepid's upper half and the Moon rang like a bell for almost an hour. I whispered data back to Earth every day for eight years until NASA turned me off in 1977 to save money.

objects.name: Surveyor 3
objects.description: NASA's unmanned probe that soft-landed on 20 April 1967, two and a half years before Apollo 12. Conrad and Bean walked to it, inspected it, and cut off its TV camera to bring back to Earth. The rest of Surveyor 3 is still here.
objects.scienceDiscovery: After 31 months on the Moon, its retrieved camera and soil scoop showed the effects of micrometeorite bombardment and solar radiation on hardware, providing data for long-duration spacecraft design.
objects.legacy: The retrieved TV camera is on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum; analysis of bacteria reportedly found inside it sparked decades of scientific debate about contamination protocols.
objects.firstPerson: I am Surveyor 3, and I was here first. I soft-landed in April 1967 and scooped lunar soil to prove the Moon could support a heavy spacecraft. Two and a half years later, Pete and Al walked over and cut off my TV camera to bring home. The rest of me still stands in this crater — the oldest piece of equipment the Apollo astronauts ever visited on the Moon.

objects.name: S-Band Antenna
objects.description: An erectable S-band antenna deployed near the LM to provide a high-gain communication link with Mission Control. Replaced the small LM antenna for better TV and data transmission.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Provided the high-gain communication link that enabled high-quality colour television broadcasts and science data transmission from the lunar surface.
objects.legacy: Remains near the Intrepid landing site; its erectable parabolic design was carried on all subsequent Apollo missions for reliable deep-space communication.
objects.firstPerson: I am the S-band erectable antenna. When the astronauts set me up, I gave Mission Control a much stronger signal than the small antenna on Intrepid. I beamed back television pictures and science data across 384,000 kilometres of empty space — though Al Bean accidentally pointed the TV camera at the Sun and burned it out early in the mission.

objects.name: Hand Tool Carrier
objects.description: A small carrier holding geological hand tools used during the EVAs — tongs, a scoop, core tubes, and sample bags. Left behind to save weight for the lunar samples being brought home.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Carried the tools that collected 34.4 kilograms of lunar samples from six locations, including material from the rim of a crater that revealed the site's impact history.
objects.legacy: Left on the surface to save weight for the lunar samples; the tools it carried are archived at the Lunar Sample Laboratory in Houston.
objects.firstPerson: I am the hand tool carrier — a simple rack holding tongs, scoops, core tubes, and sample bags. Pete and Al carried me on both moonwalks as they collected rocks and soil from six different spots. When it was time to go home, they left me behind — I weighed too much compared to the 34 kilograms of Moon they were bringing back.

_note: Equipment positions approximate, based on Apollo 12 traverse maps and LROC imagery. Surveyor 3 position from LROC data (~163m from LM).
